screens.title: Advanced C++ Features for UE5 Development
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will build a clearer mental model for three smart pointer types in Unreal, the role of lambda functions for concise inline behavior, and the delegate system that powers type-safe event handling. You will learn when exclusive ownership is safer, when shared ownership is appropriate, and how weak references avoid circular leaks. We will also contrast single-cast and multicast delegates, and explain dynamic delegates that Blueprint designers can bind to. Each concept links directly to authoring maintainable game systems. For example, a health object that multiple systems observe should live behind shared ownership so it persists exactly as long as it is needed. A multiplayer UI callback might prefer a multicast delegate so UI, audio and gameplay can all react. Finally, we will implement a small health component that uses TSharedPtr and a multicast delegate, and bind a lambda to observe health changes. This prepares you to write code that is safer, easier to reason about, and better for performance when used correctly. As we go, notice common mistakes and alternative choices and ask which pointer or delegate fits a concrete problem.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Overview
Advanced C++ Features for UE5 Development
Master ownership, inline callbacks, and event systems to write safe, maintainable game code.
16:9 HD Classroom
In this lesson
We explain TUniquePtr, TSharedPtr, TWeakPtr, lambda functions, TDelegate vs TMulticastDelegate, and dynamic delegates exposed to Blueprint. Then we implement a health component that broadcasts changes.
Why this matters
  • Memory ownership choices control lifetime and prevent leaks or premature deletes.
  • Delegates let systems communicate without hard dependencies on concrete classes.
  • Lambdas make short callbacks readable and scoped to the calling context.
Starter activity
Create a UMyHealthComponent that uses TSharedPtr for health data and a multicast delegate to notify listeners. Bind a lambda that logs health changes.
Concept map
Ownership, observation, inline behavior, and event broadcast form the toolkit for safer game code. Expect hands-on code next.
Explore Key Topics
Smart Pointers: Use the right pointer for ownership and lifetime.
Lambdas: Inline callbacks with controlled captures.
Delegates: Single or multi listeners and Blueprint exposure.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will understand the semantics of Unreal's smart pointers, how to choose between exclusive and shared ownership, and how to observe shared objects safely. You will be able to write concise lambda callbacks for immediate behaviors such as sorting or responding to a single event. You will also distinguish single-cast and multicast delegates for C++ event wiring, and know when to publish a dynamic delegate for Blueprint use. Each objective pairs a practical skill with a brief rationale: safer code prevents leaks, lambdas reduce ceremony when you need a one-off callable, and the correct delegate type reduces unnecessary runtime cost. For example, binding a multicast delegate from gameplay code allows UI and sound to react without tight coupling. Finally, you will identify common pitfalls, such as accidentally holding cycles with shared pointers or using dynamic delegates where non-dynamic delegates would be faster. These objectives prepare you to implement a small health component demonstrating smart pointers and multicast delegates.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on doing and avoiding mistakes. You will implement the UMyHealthComponent that uses a shared pointer for health data and a multicast delegate to broadcast changes. The practice forces you to instantiate TSharedPtr, mutate the shared data safely, clamp values, and broadcast proper deltas. You will also bind a lambda in BeginPlay to observe the multicast delegate and log the results. Importantly, you will learn to avoid two common pitfalls: creating circular references when shared pointers refer to each other, and choosing dynamic delegates for performance-critical C++-to-C++ events. We will practice replacing a strong shared reference with a weak reference to break cycles, and inspect when a dynamic delegate is necessary for Blueprint exposure. These hands-on skills help you produce maintainable game code and avoid subtle bugs that appear later in development or QA testing.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Practice & Pitfalls
Practice tasks and common pitfalls
Practice task: Health component
Initialize TSharedPtr health data, clamp health in ApplyDamage and ApplyHealing, and broadcast deltas using a multicast delegate. Bind a lambda in BeginPlay to log changes with UE_LOG.
Common mistakes
  • Holding mutual TSharedPtr references that form cycles and prevent destruction.
  • Using dynamic delegates for high-frequency C++ internal events, adding reflection overhead.
  • Using raw pointers where ownership semantics are unclear.
Pro tip
When two objects may reference each other, prefer a TWeakPtr in the non-owning side to avoid memory leaks and keep lifetimes explicit.
Assessment idea
Choose which pointer to use when multiple inventories share a UItem, and explain why TSharedPtr is the correct choice for shared ownership.
Outcome
You will be able to implement a robust health system and reason about delegate design for clean system integration.

screens.title: Smart Pointers Overview
screens.narratorSegment: Smart pointers provide clear ownership semantics that prevent common memory errors. TUniquePtr represents exclusive ownership: one owner is responsible for the resource and it is destroyed when that owner goes out of scope. Use TUniquePtr when a single class truly owns a resource and transferring ownership is explicit. TSharedPtr uses reference counting so many owners can hold the same object; the object is destroyed when the last shared pointer releases it. This fits situations like shared data models or objects referenced across several systems. However, shared ownership can introduce cycles. That is where TWeakPtr comes in: it observes an object managed by TSharedPtr without incrementing the reference count. You lock a weak pointer temporarily to obtain a TSharedPtr if the object still exists. A concrete example: suppose multiple UI panels reference a shared inventory model — use TSharedPtr so the model persists while panels exist, and use TWeakPtr in auxiliary systems to avoid keeping an object alive unintentionally. A common misconception is that shared pointers are always safe; they hide lifecycle complexity. Always ask who truly owns an object. Key takeaway: choose exclusive ownership when there is one clear controller; choose shared ownership when multiple parties legitimately require the resource; use weak pointers to break cycles and observe without owning.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Smart Pointers Overview
Smart Pointers Overview
Understand the intent and trade-offs of each pointer type.
TUniquePtr
Exclusive ownership. Object destroyed when the unique owner is destroyed. Good for clear single-owner resources.
TSharedPtr
Reference-counted shared ownership. Destroyed when last holder releases it. Useful for shared models across systems.
TWeakPtr
Non-owning observer of a shared object. Lock to get a temporary shared pointer if still valid.
Key Takeaway

Use ownership intent to choose a pointer: exclusive, shared, or weak observer.

Concrete example
A shared inventory model used by UI, save system, and gameplay should be TSharedPtr so it persists while any consumer exists. A tooltip system that only reads the model can hold a TWeakPtr and lock it only when needed, avoiding keeping the model alive by accident.
Common misconception
TSharedPtr eliminates all lifetime bugs. In reality, it shifts responsibility: you must still reason about cycles and ownership graphs to avoid leaks.
Check your understanding
  • When would you choose exclusive ownership over shared ownership?
  • How does a weak pointer help with circular references?

screens.title: TUniquePtr: Exclusive Ownership
screens.narratorSegment: TUniquePtr expresses exclusive ownership and deterministic destruction. Use it when one object or system is clearly responsible for a resource's lifetime. For example, a local helper object inside a component that is not shared across systems can be owned by a TUniquePtr. The pointer is destroyed automatically when the owner goes out of scope, preventing leaks without runtime overhead of reference counting. Transfer of ownership is explicit: you move the unique pointer if you need another object to take responsibility. This prevents accidental aliasing where two parts of code think they both own the same resource. A step-by-step process helps: first identify sole ownership; second allocate with MakeUnique or construct a TUniquePtr; third avoid raw pointer copies — only move when transferring ownership; fourth rely on RAII for cleanup. A common mistake is using TUniquePtr when multiple subsystems need access; in that case prefer TSharedPtr. Another pitfall is attempting to copy a unique pointer — the compiler will block this and that is a useful safety check. Key takeaway: prefer TUniquePtr for local, single-owner resources and use move semantics explicitly to transfer ownership so lifetime is always clear.

keyIdea.title: Exclusive and explicit
keyIdea.text: TUniquePtr enforces single ownership and requires explicit moves to transfer ownership, making lifetimes deterministic.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › TUniquePtr
TUniquePtr — Exclusive Ownership
Deterministic lifetime, move-only semantics, and no ref-count overhead.
Process: How to use
  1. Decide if ownership is exclusive and lifetime is bounded by a single owner.
  2. Create with MakeUnique or assign a TUniquePtr directly.
  3. Transfer ownership explicitly with MoveTemp when needed.
  4. Rely on RAII: pointer destructs automatically when owner is destroyed.
Concrete example
A helper parser instance inside a manager component that no other system needs can be owned by TUniquePtr. If the manager is destroyed, the parser is also destroyed immediately.
Key Takeaway

Use TUniquePtr when a single owner should manage lifetime and explicit moves transfer ownership safely.

Common misconception
Some developers assume unique pointers are always faster than shared pointers. They do avoid reference counting overhead, but only choose them when ownership semantics fit the problem.
Check your understanding
If two systems both need permanent access to an object, would TUniquePtr be appropriate? Why or why not?

screens.title: TSharedPtr: Shared Ownership and Reference Counting
screens.narratorSegment: TSharedPtr is designed for situations where multiple systems legitimately share ownership of a resource. It maintains an internal reference count and destroys the object only when the final shared pointer is released. This pattern simplifies code when a model or resource must persist while consumers exist, such as a shared inventory model referenced by UI, save systems, and gameplay logic. The process for using shared pointers includes: create the object with MakeShared or construct a TSharedPtr, pass copies of the pointer to interested parties, and let the reference count manage lifetime. But shared ownership requires caution: if two objects hold TSharedPtr to each other, they form a cycle that prevents destruction. To avoid cycles, identify a non-owning side and replace it with TWeakPtr. Also be mindful of performance — reference counting has a small cost compared to raw pointers or unique ownership. A misconception is treating TSharedPtr as a free replacement for raw pointers; in fact, it changes lifetime semantics and requires you to reason about ownership topology. Key takeaway: use TSharedPtr when shared life is necessary, and pair TWeakPtr when observation without ownership is required.

keyIdea.title: Share with care
keyIdea.text: TSharedPtr lets multiple owners keep an object alive, but you must design to avoid cycles and manage reference-count overhead.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › TSharedPtr
TSharedPtr — Shared Ownership
Reference counting keeps objects alive while any consumer needs them.
When to use
Use when multiple independent systems must hold references and you want automatic lifetime management.
How it works
Copies increment a reference count; destruction occurs when the count reaches zero. Create with MakeShared for efficiency.
Key Takeaway

TSharedPtr simplifies shared lifetimes but you must design ownership graphs to avoid cycles and consider the small ref-count cost.

Concrete example
A shared resource like a world-generated lookup table used by AI, rendering, and gameplay might be managed by TSharedPtr so it stays alive while at least one system needs it.
Misconception
Assuming TSharedPtr resolves all ownership uncertainty. It works, but architects must still plan reference directions to avoid leaks from cycles.
When not to use
Avoid TSharedPtr for high-frequency tight loops if a simpler ownership model exists, because ref-count operations add cost compared to raw pointers or unique ownership.

screens.title: TWeakPtr and Breaking Circular References
screens.narratorSegment: Circular references occur when two or more objects hold TSharedPtr to each other, preventing the reference count from ever reaching zero. TWeakPtr provides a lightweight solution: it watches a shared-managed object without incrementing the reference count. When you need temporary access, you lock the weak pointer to obtain a TSharedPtr if the object still exists. This pattern breaks cycles because one side of the relationship does not own the other. A concrete scenario: an inventory item and its owning container should not both strongly own each other. The container holds a TSharedPtr to items it manages; items hold a TWeakPtr back to the container if they need to query owner state. This way, when the container is destroyed and its shared pointers go away, the weak pointer does not keep it alive. A common mistake is confusing raw pointers and weak pointers; a raw pointer can dangle. TWeakPtr forces a validity check by locking before use, making code safer. Key takeaway: use TWeakPtr for non-owning observation and to break ownership cycles so objects clean up predictably. TWeakPtr and Breaking Circular References means tweakptr lets you observe shared objects safely and break cycles by avoiding increments of the reference count.. In practical terms, how weak pointers prevent shared ownership cycles. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › TWeakPtr & Cycles
TWeakPtr — Non-owning Observation
Use weak pointers to avoid cycles and to test validity before use.
When to use
Whenever a back-reference or observer is required but should not extend lifetime.
Pattern example
Container holds TSharedPtr to items; items hold TWeakPtr to the container so they can query state but do not prevent container destruction.
Key Takeaway

Use TWeakPtr for observers and to break cycles. Always lock a weak pointer before accessing the object.

Concrete code idea
Store TWeakPtr<FInventory> in items. When you need the container, call ContainerWeakPtr.Pin() and check validity before use.
Common pitfall
Using raw pointers for non-owning references can lead to dangling pointers; prefer TWeakPtr for safety when the object might be destroyed elsewhere.

screens.title: C++ Lambda Functions in UE5
screens.narratorSegment: Lambda functions are anonymous inline functions that can capture variables from their surrounding scope. They are ideal for short, local behaviors like a sorting predicate or an ad-hoc callback. In Unreal you commonly use lambdas to provide predicates for TArray::Sort, to react to an asynchronous result, or to bind a small listener inline without declaring a separate method. The capture list controls what the lambda can access: capture by value copies data into the lambda, while capture by reference captures the original variable. Be careful with captures when the lambda outlives the captured context — capturing by reference and storing the lambda for later can lead to dangling references. A concrete example: in BeginPlay you might bind a short lambda to a multicast delegate that logs health changes; capturing only the minimal data reduces risk. Another misconception is assuming lambdas eliminate the need for strong typing — they are type-safe closures but using them for large, complex logic reduces readability. Key takeaway: use lambdas for small, scoped tasks and be explicit about captures to avoid lifetime issues. C++ Lambda Functions in UE5 means lambdas give you inline functions with captured context; prefer them for short callbacks and be careful about capture lifetimes.. In practical terms, concise inline callables with controlled captures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Lambda Functions
Lambda Functions — Inline Callables
Capture local state and write short, expressive callbacks without separate function declarations.
Use cases
  • Sort predicates for TArray::Sort.
  • Short event handlers or loggers bound inline.
  • Ad-hoc transformations or filters on collections.
Safety notes
Prefer capturing by value for lambdas that may outlive local variables. Avoid capturing large objects unnecessarily to keep closures lightweight.
Key Takeaway

Lambdas are excellent for small, contextual behavior. Be explicit with captures to avoid lifetime and performance pitfalls.

Concrete example
// Sort by health descending
Array.Sort([](const FActorInfo& A, const FActorInfo& B){
  return A.Health > B.Health;
});

// Bind inline logger to multicast delegate
HealthComp->OnHealthChanged.AddLambda([](float NewHealth, float Delta){
  UE_LOG(LogTemp, Log, TEXT("New Health: %f, Delta: %f"), NewHealth, Delta);
});
Note: the code above demonstrates using a lambda as a sort predicate and as a multicast delegate listener. Ensure captured variables remain valid for the lifetime of the lambda.

screens.title: TDelegate vs TMulticastDelegate
screens.narratorSegment: Delegates provide type-safe indirection so code can call functions without hard-coding the callee. TDelegate is single-cast: it binds exactly one function or method and invoking it calls that single target. Use a TDelegate where you expect a single authoritative listener, such as a completion callback that only one owner consumes. TMulticastDelegate allows multiple bindings; broadcasting it invokes every listener in turn. This is ideal when multiple systems must react to the same event, like UI, sound, and analytics reacting to player damage. Choosing between them requires you to consider the relationship between publisher and listeners. Single-cast reduces complexity when there should be one and only one consumer; multicast is flexible for broad notifications. A common misconception is that multicast delegates impose no ordering or contract; in practice ordering may matter for side effects, so design callbacks to avoid brittle assumptions. Also, multicast delegates add minimal call overhead compared to direct function calls, but they are far more flexible for decoupling systems. Key takeaway: prefer TDelegate for single-owner callbacks and TMulticastDelegate when multiple independent consumers should respond. TDelegate vs TMulticastDelegate means use tdelegate when exactly one listener is expected; use tmulticastdelegate to broadcast to many listeners and decouple systems.. In practical terms, choosing single-cast or multi-listener delegates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Delegate Comparison
TDelegate — Single-Cast
Bind a single handler for one-to-one callbacks.
When to use
Completion callbacks, command patterns, or when there must be a single owner of the response.
Misconception
Single-cast is not 'simpler' in all cases. If you later need multiple listeners, you will need to refactor to multicast.
TMulticastDelegate — Broadcast
Multiple independent listeners can react when the publisher broadcasts.
When to use
Events like player damage should allow UI, audio, and gameplay components to all respond without hard dependencies.
Design note
Plan for listener ordering or make handlers idempotent to avoid fragile interactions when multiple listeners exist.
Key Takeaway

Choose single-cast for exclusive responses and multicast for broad notifications. Structure listeners to avoid brittle ordering dependencies.

screens.title: Dynamic Delegates and Blueprint Exposure
screens.narratorSegment: Dynamic delegates let you expose C++ events to Blueprint by using reflection-aware delegate types declared with DECLARE_DYNAMIC_ macros. This makes it possible for designers to bind Blueprint functions to events defined in C++, which is invaluable when you want non-programmers to react to gameplay events without changing code. The trade-off is additional runtime cost: dynamic delegates rely on the reflection system and have a performance overhead compared to raw C++ delegates. Expose events to Blueprint designers using reflection-aware delegate types.
When to use
When designers must bind Blueprint functions to C++ events, such as hooking up UI responses without changing code.
Performance note
Dynamic delegates use reflection and are slower than native C++ delegates. Avoid for high-frequency internal events.
Key Takeaway

Use dynamic delegates when Blueprint access is required. Keep non-dynamic delegates for internal high-performance communication.

Provide both a non-dynamic multicast delegate for C++ listeners and a dynamic multicast delegate when designers need a Blueprint hook for the same event.

Don’t default to dynamic delegates for everything. They are convenient, but unnecessary for pure C++ systems and add reflection overhead.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › UMyHealthComponent Walkthrough
Code walkthrough
The starter header defines FHealthData, a multicast delegate, and a TSharedPtr member. Implement the constructor, ApplyDamage, ApplyHealing, and GetCurrentHealth. Then bind a lambda in the actor's BeginPlay to log results.
// MyHealthComponent.cpp (implementation highlights)
UMyHealthComponent::UMyHealthComponent()
{
  // Initialize shared health data with MaxHealth = 100.0f
  HealthData = MakeShared<FHealthData>(100.0f);
}

void UMyHealthComponent::ApplyDamage(float DamageAmount)
{
  if(!HealthData.IsValid()) return;
  HealthData->CurrentHealth = FMath::Max(0.0f, HealthData->CurrentHealth - DamageAmount);
  OnHealthChanged.Broadcast(HealthData->CurrentHealth, -DamageAmount);
}

void UMyHealthComponent::ApplyHealing(float HealAmount)
{
  if(!HealthData.IsValid()) return;
  HealthData->CurrentHealth = FMath::Min(HealthData->MaxHealth, HealthData->CurrentHealth + HealAmount);
  OnHealthChanged.Broadcast(HealthData->CurrentHealth, HealAmount);
}

float UMyHealthComponent::GetCurrentHealth() const
{
  return HealthData.IsValid() ? HealthData->CurrentHealth : 0.0f;
}

// In AMyGameCharacter::BeginPlay()
if(HealthComp)
{
  HealthComp->OnHealthChanged.AddLambda([](float NewHealth, float Delta){
    UE_LOG(LogTemp, Log, TEXT("New Health: %f, Delta: %f"), NewHealth, Delta);
  });
}
Runtime expectation
When you call ApplyDamage(20) then ApplyHealing(10), the log should show: 
LogTemp: New Health: 80.000000, Delta: -20.000000
LogTemp: New Health: 90.000000, Delta: 10.000000
This confirms the delegate broadcast and lambda binding worked.
Misconception check
If HealthData were a raw pointer and the component was destroyed while another system still accessed it, you could crash. TSharedPtr avoids that by ensuring the data stays alive while holders exist.
Debugging tips
  • Check HealthData.IsValid() before dereferencing.
  • Confirm delegates are bound in BeginPlay and not before components are initialized.
  • Use UE_LOG to verify broadcast flow and payload values.
Try this
Modify the component to use a TWeakPtr for a back-reference to its owner and ensure you Pin() before use.
Key Takeaway

Implement shared data and multicast delegates carefully, test broadcasts with logging, and guard pointer validity to avoid crashes.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the first group of key concepts. TUniquePtr provides exclusive ownership with deterministic destruction and requires move semantics to transfer ownership. TSharedPtr uses reference counting to enable shared ownership so an object persists while any owner exists, but you must design around cycles to avoid leaks. TWeakPtr observes a shared-managed object without contributing to the reference count and must be locked to obtain a temporary shared pointer. These three pointer types form the core tools for memory and lifetime management in Unreal C++ and choosing between them depends on ownership intent and lifetime topology. Keep in mind concrete examples: single-owner helper objects for unique pointers, shared data models for shared pointers, and back-references for weak pointers. If you can explain these three choices and give a scenario for each, you are well-positioned to design safe object lifetimes in your UE5 code.

Exclusive ownership. Object is destroyed when the owning pointer is destroyed.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will build a clearer mental model for three smart pointer types in Unreal, the role of lambda functions for concise inline behavior, and the delegate system that powers type-safe event handling. You will learn when exclusive ownership is safer, when shared ownership is appropriate, and how weak references avoid circular leaks. We will also contrast single-cast and multicast delegates, and explain dynamic delegates that Blueprint designers can bind to. Each concept links directly to authoring maintainable game systems. For example, a health object that multiple systems observe should live behind shared ownership so it persists exactly as long as it is needed. A multiplayer UI callback might prefer a multicast delegate so UI, audio and gameplay can all react. Finally, we will implement a small health component that uses TSharedPtr and a multicast delegate, and bind a lambda to observe health changes. This prepares you to write code that is safer, easier to reason about, and better for performance when used correctly. As we go, notice common mistakes and alternative choices and ask which pointer or delegate fits a concrete problem.

By the end of this chapter you will understand the semantics of Unreal's smart pointers, how to choose between exclusive and shared ownership, and how to observe shared objects safely. You will be able to write concise lambda callbacks for immediate behaviors such as sorting or responding to a single event. You will also distinguish single-cast and multicast delegates for C++ event wiring, and know when to publish a dynamic delegate for Blueprint use. Each objective pairs a practical skill with a brief rationale: safer code prevents leaks, lambdas reduce ceremony when you need a one-off callable, and the correct delegate type reduces unnecessary runtime cost. For example, binding a multicast delegate from gameplay code allows UI and sound to react without tight coupling. Finally, you will identify common pitfalls, such as accidentally holding cycles with shared pointers or using dynamic delegates where non-dynamic delegates would be faster. These objectives prepare you to implement a small health component demonstrating smart pointers and multicast delegates.

These objectives focus on doing and avoiding mistakes. You will implement the UMyHealthComponent that uses a shared pointer for health data and a multicast delegate to broadcast changes. The practice forces you to instantiate TSharedPtr, mutate the shared data safely, clamp values, and broadcast proper deltas. You will also bind a lambda in BeginPlay to observe the multicast delegate and log the results. Importantly, you will learn to avoid two common pitfalls: creating circular references when shared pointers refer to each other, and choosing dynamic delegates for performance-critical C++-to-C++ events. We will practice replacing a strong shared reference with a weak reference to break cycles, and inspect when a dynamic delegate is necessary for Blueprint exposure. These hands-on skills help you produce maintainable game code and avoid subtle bugs that appear later in development or QA testing.

Smart pointers provide clear ownership semantics that prevent common memory errors. TUniquePtr represents exclusive ownership: one owner is responsible for the resource and it is destroyed when that owner goes out of scope. Use TUniquePtr when a single class truly owns a resource and transferring ownership is explicit. TSharedPtr uses reference counting so many owners can hold the same object; the object is destroyed when the last shared pointer releases it. This fits situations like shared data models or objects referenced across several systems. However, shared ownership can introduce cycles. That is where TWeakPtr comes in: it observes an object managed by TSharedPtr without incrementing the reference count. You lock a weak pointer temporarily to obtain a TSharedPtr if the object still exists. A concrete example: suppose multiple UI panels reference a shared inventory model — use TSharedPtr so the model persists while panels exist, and use TWeakPtr in auxiliary systems to avoid keeping an object alive unintentionally. A common misconception is that shared pointers are always safe; they hide lifecycle complexity. Always ask who truly owns an object. Key takeaway: choose exclusive ownership when there is one clear controller; choose shared ownership when multiple parties legitimately require the resource; use weak pointers to break cycles and observe without owning.

TUniquePtr expresses exclusive ownership and deterministic destruction. Use it when one object or system is clearly responsible for a resource's lifetime. For example, a local helper object inside a component that is not shared across systems can be owned by a TUniquePtr. The pointer is destroyed automatically when the owner goes out of scope, preventing leaks without runtime overhead of reference counting. Transfer of ownership is explicit: you move the unique pointer if you need another object to take responsibility. This prevents accidental aliasing where two parts of code think they both own the same resource. A step-by-step process helps: first identify sole ownership; second allocate with MakeUnique or construct a TUniquePtr; third avoid raw pointer copies — only move when transferring ownership; fourth rely on RAII for cleanup. A common mistake is using TUniquePtr when multiple subsystems need access; in that case prefer TSharedPtr. Another pitfall is attempting to copy a unique pointer — the compiler will block this and that is a useful safety check. Key takeaway: prefer TUniquePtr for local, single-owner resources and use move semantics explicitly to transfer ownership so lifetime is always clear.

TSharedPtr is designed for situations where multiple systems legitimately share ownership of a resource. It maintains an internal reference count and destroys the object only when the final shared pointer is released. This pattern simplifies code when a model or resource must persist while consumers exist, such as a shared inventory model referenced by UI, save systems, and gameplay logic. The process for using shared pointers includes: create the object with MakeShared or construct a TSharedPtr, pass copies of the pointer to interested parties, and let the reference count manage lifetime. But shared ownership requires caution: if two objects hold TSharedPtr to each other, they form a cycle that prevents destruction. To avoid cycles, identify a non-owning side and replace it with TWeakPtr. Also be mindful of performance — reference counting has a small cost compared to raw pointers or unique ownership. A misconception is treating TSharedPtr as a free replacement for raw pointers; in fact, it changes lifetime semantics and requires you to reason about ownership topology. Key takeaway: use TSharedPtr when shared life is necessary, and pair TWeakPtr when observation without ownership is required.

Circular references occur when two or more objects hold TSharedPtr to each other, preventing the reference count from ever reaching zero. TWeakPtr provides a lightweight solution: it watches a shared-managed object without incrementing the reference count. When you need temporary access, you lock the weak pointer to obtain a TSharedPtr if the object still exists. This pattern breaks cycles because one side of the relationship does not own the other. A concrete scenario: an inventory item and its owning container should not both strongly own each other. The container holds a TSharedPtr to items it manages; items hold a TWeakPtr back to the container if they need to query owner state. This way, when the container is destroyed and its shared pointers go away, the weak pointer does not keep it alive. A common mistake is confusing raw pointers and weak pointers; a raw pointer can dangle. TWeakPtr forces a validity check by locking before use, making code safer. Key takeaway: use TWeakPtr for non-owning observation and to break ownership cycles so objects clean up predictably. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Lambda functions are anonymous inline functions that can capture variables from their surrounding scope. They are ideal for short, local behaviors like a sorting predicate or an ad-hoc callback. In Unreal you commonly use lambdas to provide predicates for TArray::Sort, to react to an asynchronous result, or to bind a small listener inline without declaring a separate method. The capture list controls what the lambda can access: capture by value copies data into the lambda, while capture by reference captures the original variable. Be careful with captures when the lambda outlives the captured context — capturing by reference and storing the lambda for later can lead to dangling references. A concrete example: in BeginPlay you might bind a short lambda to a multicast delegate that logs health changes; capturing only the minimal data reduces risk. Another misconception is assuming lambdas eliminate the need for strong typing — they are type-safe closures but using them for large, complex logic reduces readability. Key takeaway: use lambdas for small, scoped tasks and be explicit about captures to avoid lifetime issues. Delegates provide type-safe indirection so code can call functions without hard-coding the callee. TDelegate is single-cast: it binds exactly one function or method and invoking it calls that single target. Use a TDelegate where you expect a single authoritative listener, such as a completion callback that only one owner consumes. TMulticastDelegate allows multiple bindings; broadcasting it invokes every listener in turn. This is ideal when multiple systems must react to the same event, like UI, sound, and analytics reacting to player damage. Choosing between them requires you to consider the relationship between publisher and listeners. Single-cast reduces complexity when there should be one and only one consumer; multicast is flexible for broad notifications. A common misconception is that multicast delegates impose no ordering or contract; in practice ordering may matter for side effects, so design callbacks to avoid brittle assumptions. Also, multicast delegates add minimal call overhead compared to direct function calls, but they are far more flexible for decoupling systems.
